stories.title: Ethiopia: Call for a Special Session to Prevent Further Atrocities
stories.summary: Ethiopia: Call for a Special Session to Prevent Further Atrocities 9 October 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) Civil society joint letter to the United Nations Human Rights Council To Permanent Representatives of Member and Observer States of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Council (Geneva, Switzerland) 8 October 2026 Ethiopia: The Human Rights Council should convene a special session to address the quickly deteriorating human rights situation and prevent further atrocity crimes Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Excellencies, As armed hostilities have resumed on a large scale in Ethiopia, with risks of repetition of the atrocity crimes documented during the 2020-2022 conflict, we, the undersigned civil society organisations, urge the Human Rights Council to urgently convene a special session on the human rights impact of the conflict. At the session, we urge the adoption of a resolution requesting the Council's President to appoint an advisory panel of experts, drawn from the pool of existing independent UN and African human rights experts, to undertake a swift assessment, compile a summary report, and make recommendations on steps the Council could take to address the human rights situation in Ethiopia. The Council should stand ready to take further action, as appropriate, to address any developments in Ethiopia or the sub-region, send a message of deterrence to all actors, and indicate that those responsible for perpetrating, ordering or facilitating violations should be held accountable. On 22 September 2026, after long-simmering tensions between the Ethiopian Federal Government led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated from sporadic clashes and airstrikes to open military confrontation, fighting resumed on a large scale and spread to the Afar and Amhara regions in northern Ethiopia. Heavy fighting, involving the use of drone strikes, mortar strikes and artillery fire, including indiscriminate airstrikes in populated areas and on civilian infrastructure that may amount to war crimes, is pitting federal forces, the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), and allied forces against not only the TPLF's Tigray Defence Force (TDF) but other regional armed groups, including the Amhara Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), both of which formed an alliance with TPLF and other regional groupings to topple the federal government.

stories.title: Eswatini: Eswatini Repatriation of U.S. Deportees Raises Concerns

Eswatini has repatriated 10 individuals - some with criminal records - probably via Johannesburg to third countries, but both countries are denying that Eswatini was "secretly releasing United States (US) deportees at night to South Africa through informal border crossings..." The 10 deportees are part of 31 people who have been deported to the country from the US since 2025. Though officials said the 10 were very likely to have transited through South Africa, Eswatini government acting spokesperson Thabile Mdluli told Daily Maverick, "We are deliberately not mentioning the countries of transit. We will still need them for future repatriations." The media reports that Eswatini had smuggled US deportees into South Africa seem to originate from the online news portal Swaziland News, which is notorious for publishing similar kinds of stories. Reports 'misleading' The Eswatini government responded in a statement expressing concern about the reports, which it said were misleading "and have the potential to cause unnecessary apprehension and anxiety, particularly among neighbouring countries." Building on more than 50 years of U.S. health assistance to Zambia, this MOU represents a $2.49 billion partnership of $1.52 billion in planned U.S. health assistance and a commitment from Zambia to invest $975 million in new funding in its own health system over five years. Under this MOU, the United States also plans to provide more than $13 million in Global Health Security funding to strengthen Zambia’s ability to detect and respond to infectious disease threats. Over five years, Zambia will progressively assume greater responsibility for its health system, including the procurement of health commodities, transitioning U.S.-supported frontline health workers into its civil service, and strengthening systems to track medicines and supplies from production to delivery. The United States will support Zambia in modernizing its health infrastructure, to include expanding electronic medical records and interoperable data systems for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and disease outbreak surveillance.

stories.summary: Burundi: la prorogation du mandat du Rapporteur spécial de l’ONU «montre que la situation du pays n'est pas oubliée» Le Conseil des droits de l'homme des Nations unies a maintenu le 6 octobre 2026 sa surveillance du Burundi en vue notamment de la présidentielle de mai 2027, s'inquiétant d'une « augmentation alarmante du nombre d'exécutions extrajudiciaires et de disparitions forcées ». stories.title: Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
stories.summary: Image source, Zanu-PF Image caption, Wicknell Chivayo, who had a fleet of personalised luxury cars, loved white Rolls-Royces By Ish Mafundikwa Reporting from Harare Published 8 October 2026 Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death. He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes. He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving. Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes. His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune.

stories.title: Africa: Africa's Non-Communicable Diseases Burden Continues to Rise, Latest Study Finds
stories.summary: Africa's Non-Communicable Diseases Burden Continues to Rise, Latest Study Finds 5 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) A 2026 Lancet Global Health analysis using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 data finds that non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are accounting for a growing share of Africa's health burden. In 2023, NCDs resulted in an estimated 263 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), with one DALY representing one year of healthy life lost. NCDs caused an estimated 2.33 billion cases and 4.70 million deaths. The leading causes of NCD deaths in 2023 were, Ischaemic heart disease - 801,000 deaths, stroke - 700,000, chronic kidney disease - 293,000, hypertensive heart disease - 246,000 and diabetes - 245,000. The three largest contributors to NCD deaths were high systolic blood pressure - 26.2% dietary risks - 14.7%, air pollution - 14.2%.

stories.title: ‘There’s always been a belittling of African women’: honouring history’s invisible heroines
stories.summary: As demand for it drove the transatlantic slave trade, sugar symbolises the sacrifice of people for goods. Photograph: Pamela Tulizo Congolese photographer Pamela Tulizo uses costume and vivid scenery to celebrate women’s strength and give a new perspective on slavery By Sarah Johnson P amela Tulizo’s latest series of photographs started with a question. “I asked myself, why are women in my community in particular, and African women in general, so strong?” says Tulizo, an artist and photographer from the Democratic Republic of the Congo . “Where does this strength come from?” Growing up in Goma in eastern DRC, Tulizo was informed and inspired by the women she was surrounded by, including her mother, her sisters, her mother’s friends and her neighbours. Years later, when she began to look into the role of women throughout African history, she says: “I realised that perhaps women have been forced to be strong since the dawn of time, forced by circumstance to build that resilience.” View image in fullscreen Women are placed at the centre of the series of 23 staged photographs Her research brought her to slavery, the “cruellest period in human history”, which is often just associated with the men who were forced across oceans to form workforces abroad. Women, she noticed, were largely invisible, their stories untold. With that in mind, Tulizo placed women at the centre of her series of 23 staged photographs called Mababu (“ancestors” in Swahili).

stories.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed

Photograph: DEA/F Guenet/De Agostini/Getty Images Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls. The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC. Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

stories.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere across Africa?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NTaF The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agents Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic , Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled " Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI ," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported. The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world. Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.

stories.title: Morocco's first female head of government: Symbol or real reform?

We've never had one [a female head of government] before," said another. "May God bless her and help her stay on a straight path." stories.title: The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'

"Especially when they are both drunk." "I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her." Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa. The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township. "Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am." At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust. At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
